S1.title: Apache Spark compute for Data Engineering and Data Science in Microsoft Fabric
claims: Fabric runs Data Engineering and Data Science workloads on a fully managed Apache Spark platform offering two pool styles: starter pools that are preconfigured for near-instant startup, and custom Spark pools that workspace admins tune for node size, scaling, and other compute settings.

Starter pool sessions typically begin in 5 to 10 seconds because Fabric keeps Medium-node clusters pre-provisioned and always running; selecting any other node size or custom compute configuration switches the session to on-demand provisioning, which takes roughly 2 to 5 minutes.

Environment library publishing mode changes session personalization time: Quick mode installs libraries at session start adding about 30 seconds to 5 minutes, Full mode deploys an environment snapshot adding roughly 1 to 3 minutes, and Full mode combined with a custom live pool pre-bakes the snapshot onto hydrated clusters so sessions can start in about 5 seconds.

Workspaces using Tenant Private Links or Managed VNets cannot use starter pools at all; Fabric must create the cluster on demand, adding 2 to 5 minutes to session startup, plus any additional library personalization time.

Spark billing in Fabric covers only the period a notebook or job session is actively running: idle pre-warmed cluster time, cluster acquisition, Spark context initialization, and post-job deallocation are all unbilled for both starter and custom pools.

Each Fabric capacity unit grants two Spark vCores, and a 3x burst multiplier applies on top; an F64 SKU therefore exposes 384 Spark vCores (64 CU x 2 x 3), which caps the total vCores a custom Spark pool can be configured with.

Custom pool node sizes range from Small (4 vCores, 32 GB) through Medium (8/64), Large (16/128), X-Large (32/256) to XX-Large (64 vCores, 512 GB); the two largest sizes are restricted to non-trial Fabric SKUs, and changing node size after creation requires restarting active sessions.

A Fabric Spark pool instance consists of one head node plus workers: the head node hosts Livy, the YARN Resource Manager, ZooKeeper, and the Spark driver, every node runs a Node Agent and YARN Node Manager, and each worker runs the Spark Executor service.

Fabric fixes the node-to-executor ratio at 1:1 — one node is dedicated to the driver and each remaining node hosts exactly one executor — except in single-node pools, where the driver and executor split the node's resources in half (a setup with restorable HA aimed at small workloads).

Autoscale scales a pool between configured minimum and maximum node counts based on activity, and Fabric sets spark.yarn.executor.decommission.enabled to true by default so underused nodes shut down automatically; setting it to false makes scale-down less aggressive.

With dynamic allocation enabled, Fabric reserves executors at job submission based on the pool's minimum node count, then grows executor count when tasks outstrip current capacity and releases executors as work completes or the application idles — relieving users from hand-tuning executor counts per job stage.

Sessions expire after 20 minutes by default (configurable), an unused pool is deallocated 2 minutes after session expiry, and a regular custom pool takes about three minutes to start because nodes must be acquired from Azure.

S2.title: Native execution engine for Fabric Data Engineering
claims: Fabric's native execution engine (NEE) is built on two open-source components: Velox, a C++ database acceleration library from Meta that performs vectorized execution, and Apache Gluten (incubating), a middle layer from Intel that offloads execution from JVM-based SQL engines to native engines.

Gluten intercepts the optimized Spark SQL physical plan and converts supported portions into a Substrait plan, which Velox then executes as vectorized, SIMD-accelerated, columnar C++ code in place of the JVM operator implementations.

When NEE encounters an operator, expression, data type, or feature it doesn't support, the affected segment of the query automatically falls back to the standard JVM Spark engine rather than failing the job; execution continues correctly but without native acceleration for that portion.

As of the current NEE release, structured streaming, ANSI SQL mode, and JSON/XML source formats are not accelerated and always execute on JVM Spark; Python and Scala UDFs and complex types (arrays, maps, structs) are now supported natively, and CSV is now handled through a vectorized native parser rather than falling back.

NEE preserves Fabric Spark's existing query optimizer behaviors — adaptive query execution, cost-based rewrites, column pruning, and predicate pushdown — so these still apply even to queries where some operators are offloaded to the native path and others fall back to the JVM.

NEE supports parallel Delta snapshot loading and accelerates read operations on Delta tables organized with Z-ordering or Liquid Clustering, giving additional gains on top of raw operator vectorization when the underlying data layout is optimized.

NEE casting from DECIMAL to FLOAT diverges from vanilla Spark: Spark preserves precision by round-tripping the value through a string conversion, while Velox casts directly from the internal int128_t representation, which can produce different rounding results for the same input.

The round() function can return different results under NEE than under vanilla Spark because Velox implements it using the C++ standard library's std::round rather than replicating Spark's own rounding logic, a source of subtle numeric inconsistency worth testing for before relying on NEE in precision-sensitive pipelines.

collect_list() and collect_set() use ARRAY as their intermediate aggregation type under NEE, whereas vanilla Spark uses BINARY; this type mismatch can cause query-planning or execution compatibility issues in mixed or migrated workloads that assume Spark's default intermediate representation.

When spark.sql.mapKeyDedupPolicy is set to EXCEPTION, vanilla Spark throws an error on duplicate keys passed to map(), but NEE currently skips this duplicate-key check entirely and silently returns a result keyed on the last-seen value instead of failing.

Whether an operator actually executed on the native path can be confirmed via Spark UI or df.explain() output — native operators carry suffixes like *Transformer, *NativeFileScan, or *VeloxColumnarToRowExec — or via the dedicated 'Gluten SQL / DataFrame' tab and its query execution graph, where green nodes denote native execution and light blue nodes denote JVM fallback.

Independent GA benchmark results reported by the Fabric product team showed roughly 4x faster query execution on a 1 TB TPC-DS workload versus vanilla Spark, and up to 6x end-to-end improvement on representative big-data jobs and typical aggregation/join queries, with NEE included at no additional cost over standard Spark capacity billing.

S3.title: Optimize Delta Lake tables with V-Order in Fabric
claims: V-Order is a write-time optimization for Parquet files that improves downstream read performance across Fabric engines; it pays off most in read-heavy patterns like dashboarding, interactive analytics, and repeated scans.

Internally, V-Order reorganizes the physical Parquet layout at write time — adjusting row-group distribution, encoding choices, and compression — rather than changing the logical data, which is why it speeds up reads without altering query semantics.
V-Ordered files remain fully compliant with the open-source Parquet specification, so any standard Parquet reader can consume them; non-Fabric engines simply do not get the read acceleration.
Microsoft states the typical V-Order tradeoff as writes taking roughly 15% longer on average, in exchange for reads that can improve significantly depending on the workload.

V-Order is disabled by default in all newly created Fabric workspaces (spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default=false), a deliberate default that favors write-heavy ingestion and transformation pipelines over read optimization.

V-Order can be controlled at three levels: the Spark session config spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default, the Delta table property delta.parquet.vorder.enabled, and the per-write DataFrame writer option parquet.vorder.enabled.

Session and write-level V-Order settings take precedence over the table property: enabling V-Order for a session applies it to every Parquet write in that session, including Delta tables whose delta.parquet.vorder.enabled property is explicitly false, and even non-Delta Parquet writes.

Toggling the V-Order table property only affects future writes; files already on disk keep the layout they were written with, so applying or removing V-Order on existing data requires a physical rewrite via table compaction (OPTIMIZE).

For read-heavy workloads, enable V-Order either by setting spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default to true for the session or by selecting the readHeavyforSpark or ReadHeavy Spark resource profiles, which turn V-Order on automatically.

Leaving V-Order enabled on write-dominated ingestion or transformation pipelines is counterproductive: the write penalty is paid on every job while the read-side benefit goes unused; disable it at session level for such workloads.

Fabric Runtime 1.3 removed the legacy spark.sql.parquet.vorder.enable setting; code migrated from earlier runtimes should drop it, since V-Order can instead be applied during Delta OPTIMIZE compaction.

In an overwrite using a replaceWhere predicate, V-Order is applied only to the files actually rewritten by that predicate, not to the whole table; V-Order is file-level and composes with Delta features like Z-Order, compaction, vacuum, and time travel.

S4.title: A Deep Dive into Optimized Write in Microsoft Fabric
claims: Optimized Write addresses the small file problem by shuffling data across executors before writing, so each partition is handled by a single executor and produces fewer, larger files rather than many small ones scattered across the cluster.

The target file size for Optimized Write is governed by the BinSize configuration key; in Fabric the default is 1 GB, integer values are interpreted as megabytes, and the recommended tuning values are 256 MB for general workloads or 128 MB for small workloads to avoid over-consolidation.

The Optimized Write configuration key changed between Fabric Spark runtimes: Runtime 1.2 used spark.microsoft.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled, while Runtime 1.3 and later uses spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled.

In the author's benchmark on a highly partitioned table (1,823 date-sold partitions), enabling Optimized Write reduced write time from roughly 6 minutes 43 seconds to 53 seconds and cut file count from 175,008 to 1,823, yielding a 19x improvement in downstream query duration — results attributed to the author's controlled test environment.

On a non-partitioned table in the author's benchmark, disabling Optimized Write produced 35% faster writes and 2x faster queries because 96 output files offered better read parallelism across the available executor cores than the 15 files produced when the feature was enabled — showing the feature can hurt non-partitioned workloads.
Optimized Write is functionally incompatible with Liquid Clustering and should be disabled for tables using that feature.

For streaming jobs that produce micro-batches, Optimized Write is recommended because each micro-batch naturally generates many small files; enabling the feature consolidates those files at write time rather than requiring a separate compaction step.

A 1 GB BinSize target is recommended when writing Delta tables that back Power BI Direct Lake semantic models, because larger files align with the Direct Lake loading pattern and reduce the number of segment loads needed.

When UPDATE or MERGE operations are combined with deletion vectors enabled on a Delta table, the probability of generating small files remains high even with Optimized Write active, because those operations touch many existing files and create new ones for changed records.

Fragmented writes caused by the small file problem measurably degrade Parquet compression efficiency; in the author's partitioned benchmark, the feature-disabled variant produced roughly 33% more data on disk than the Optimized Write variant.

S5.title: Mastering Spark: The Art and Science of Table Compaction
claims: Auto Compaction in Delta Lake triggers automatically after write operations when the number of small files in a table partition exceeds a configurable threshold, merging undersized files into larger ones without requiring a scheduled job.

Auto Compaction is controlled by three tunable properties: maxFileSize (default 128 MB, the target for compacted files), minFileSize (default unset, calculated as half of maxFileSize at runtime — files below this are candidates), and minNumFiles (default 50, the count of undersized files that must exist before compaction fires).

Auto Compaction operations are distinguishable from manual OPTIMIZE runs in the Delta transaction log: the operationParameters field includes an 'auto' flag set to true for system-triggered compactions, which is useful for auditing compaction history in Fabric.

In the author's benchmark using 200 iterations of 1K-row batch writes, combining Auto Compaction with Optimized Write achieved the best outcome across all five tested configurations: lowest total runtime (12.77 minutes), lowest file-count variance (standard deviation of 14), and consistent query durations.

In the same benchmark, running no compaction at all produced the worst result by a wide margin: 33.27 minutes total runtime and a file-count standard deviation of 864, demonstrating that unmanaged small file accumulation severely degrades pipeline performance over time.

Optimized Write alone (without post-write compaction) reduced per-iteration file output from roughly 16 files to 1 file in the 1K-batch scenario with negligible overhead, but scheduled compaction or Auto Compaction is still needed over time to consolidate files into the 500 MB to 1 GB range for long-term read performance.

A bug in earlier versions of Fabric Spark Runtime caused Auto Compaction to trigger excessively on tables exceeding 1 GB because the implementation counted already-compacted files toward the minNumFiles threshold rather than only undersized files; the author recommended falling back to scheduled OPTIMIZE for tables larger than 1 GB until the fix shipped. Microsoft subsequently resolved the issue in the Fabric Spark Runtime.

For tables smaller than 1 GB, Auto Compaction alone is sufficient for file management; for larger tables, the recommended long-term strategy is to combine Auto Compaction with periodic ad-hoc OPTIMIZE runs targeting 500 MB to 1 GB file sizes to handle files that auto-compaction leaves undersized.

The author recommends enabling Auto Compaction as a default practice because the configuration overhead is minimal and it consistently produces stable file counts and query latencies across varied batch sizes without requiring scheduling logic.

S6.title: From Imperative to Declarative: How Data Engineering Found a Better Way
claims: Microsoft Fabric Materialized Lake Views entered preview in May 2025 and reached general availability in March 2026, providing a platform-native declarative transformation capability analogous to Databricks Lakeflow and Snowflake Dynamic Tables.

Spark Declarative Pipelines, contributed to Apache Spark by Databricks in June 2025, shipped as a headline feature in Spark 4.1.0 released in December 2025. This brings execution-level declarativeness to the open-source Spark runtime itself, not only to platform-specific wrappers.

Procedural PySpark notebooks are well suited to genuinely complex logic — API ingestion, streaming workloads, ML inference, iterative algorithms, and deeply nested data structures — where declarative SQL expressions would be insufficient or unnatural. Declarative frameworks deliberately do not try to replace notebooks in these domains.

Interface-level declarative tools such as dbt compile developer-authored SQL models into execution plans but still issue imperative mutations at runtime, making them analogous to build systems like Make. Execution-level tools such as SQLMesh go further by exposing a plan-and-apply workflow that shows the exact changes before they run and supports isolated virtual-environment testing.

Declarative transformation frameworks resolve inter-table dependencies automatically and validate the dependency graph at compile time rather than at runtime. This contrasts with procedural notebooks, where dependencies are implied by cell execution order and errors only surface during a run.

For stable, SQL-expressible business logic in Fabric, the recommended approach is to use native Materialized Lake Views for low operational overhead or dbt for richer testing, CI/CD integration, and cross-platform portability. Neither choice requires migrating the entire pipeline simultaneously; a single staging layer or subject area is a practical starting point.

When LLM-generated code is used to build data pipelines, declarative frameworks offer a structural safety net: declarations are validated at compile time before execution, and tools such as dbt's dry-run mode and Spark SDP's --dry-run flag surface generation errors before they reach production data.

Declarative ingestion tools — including Fivetran, Airbyte, and Fabric Copy Job — manage schema evolution and incremental-state tracking declaratively, removing the need for hand-written change-detection logic in ingestion pipelines. Fivetran merged with dbt Labs in October 2025, unifying extract-load and transform ownership under a single vendor.

S7.title: Can You Actually Build a Production Fabric Platform with Private Links?
claims: Fabric offers two distinct private link scopes: a tenant-level option covering the entire tenant at any paid SKU, generally available since May 2024, and a workspace-level option restricted to individual workspaces on F SKUs only, generally available since October 2025. The tenant-level model is all-or-nothing; the workspace-level model permits a mixed public-private deployment.

On-premises data gateways cannot register and will not function when tenant-level Block Public Internet Access is enabled. There is no supported configuration for using on-premises data gateways alongside tenant-level private links; the only replacement is a VNet data gateway, which requires Azure networking infrastructure such as ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN.

At the workspace level, Fabric SQL Database, Deployment Pipelines, shortcut transforms, and the Power Platform Dataflow Connector are all unsupported when public access is blocked on the workspace. These are design-level constraints, not configuration gaps, and are unlikely to be resolved by minor product updates.

Direct Lake connections fail when the Block Public Internet Access tenant setting is active. Semantic models relying on Direct Lake mode must route through public endpoints, making this connection mode incompatible with the most restrictive Fabric network isolation posture.

Provisioning a new capacity while tenant-level private links are active can take up to 24 hours to propagate into the private DNS zone. The tenant-level private link configuration also blocks tenant migrations entirely for the duration it is enabled.

Enabling a managed VNet for Spark increases cold-start times to the 3–5 minute range and disables Spark starter pools entirely. Workspace regional migration is also blocked once a managed VNet has been allocated to a workspace.

Several Power BI features are unavailable when private links or public-access blocking is in effect: Publish to Web, email subscriptions, PDF and PowerPoint export, and Copilot under tenant-level private links are all unsupported. Power BI modern usage metrics are only partially available under tenant-level private links, capturing Report Open events but not Page Views or performance data.

Pipeline copy activity to and from Fabric Data Warehouse is unsupported when private links are enabled. Eventhouse is also unsupported as a direct pipeline copy destination under both tenant-level and workspace-level private link configurations.

For organisations that lack an explicit regulatory mandate for network-level isolation, Conditional Access combined with an IP firewall addresses the dominant risk surface — identity, device compliance, and network location — without the operational constraints imposed by private links. Conditional Access cannot target Fabric in isolation and must cover all dependent service endpoints.

Private links are a viable architectural choice only for pure cloud-to-cloud workloads on F SKUs that have no dependency on on-premises data sources, Deployment Pipelines, or Fabric SQL Database, and where Power BI feature limitations are operationally acceptable.
